title: Total approved minutes

Keep one running total, initially zero.
For each duration, add it only when duration >= minimum.

Inspect each duration once. The comparison includes equality, so a session exactly at the minimum must be added. Returning zero also handles both an empty input and an input with no qualifying sessions.

title: Fit consecutive costs into a budget
statement: Return the longest length of a consecutive stretch whose sum is at most budget. An empty stretch is allowed, so return zero if no entry can fit.
constraints: Python 3.11+. Do not mutate any input. All integer inputs exclude bool. Lists and strings have at most 1,000 elements or characters unless stated otherwise.
Costs and budget are nonnegative integers from 0 to 10,000. Negative costs are outside the contract.
hints: Expand a stretch one entry at a time and track its sum.
If the sum exceeds budget, remove entries from the left until it fits.
Nonnegative costs make shrinking safe; record right - left + 1 after restoring the budget.
approach: After adding a new right endpoint, discard leftmost entries until the sum is affordable. Because costs are nonnegative, adding later entries cannot rescue an over-budget earlier start.
Once the sum fits, this is the longest affordable stretch ending at that right endpoint. Both endpoints move only forward, so repeated shrinking still makes linear progress.
solution:
def affordable_stretch(costs: list[int], budget: int) -> int:
    left = 0
    current = 0
    best = 0
    for right, cost in enumerate(costs):
        current += cost
        while current > budget:
            current -= costs[left]
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Each entry enters and leaves the window at most once.
pitfalls: Using this method with negative costs invalidates the elimination argument.
Forgetting that zero-cost entries can extend a zero-budget stretch.
transfer: Now allow negative credits. Construct an example where this shrinking rule misses the best stretch before choosing another approach.

Compare timestamps, not reading values or row positions.
Replace when the device is new or timestamp >= its stored timestamp.
approach: After each input row, the dictionary holds the winning sample among rows seen for each device. An older timestamp cannot replace that winner.
Equality must replace the stored sample because the contract favors the later row. Build a fresh two-element list for each stored result rather than returning a mutable input row.
complexity: Expected O(n + c) time for n rows and c device-name characters; O(u) output entries for u devices.
pitfalls: Taking the last row without checking its timestamp.
Using > and retaining the wrong row on a timestamp tie.
transfer: Keep the two most recent distinct timestamps per device. Specify which reading wins when one timestamp repeats.

title: Combine maintenance coverage
statement: Each [start, end] is a half-open time interval with start < end. Return sorted coverage intervals, combining overlaps and touching intervals. For example [1,3] and [3,5] become [1,5]. Do not change the supplied rows.
constraints: Python 3.11+. Do not mutate any input. All integer inputs exclude bool. Lists and strings have at most 1,000 elements or characters unless stated otherwise.
Every row has two integer endpoints with 0 <= start < end <= 1,000,000. Input may be unsorted or repeated.
hints: Arrange intervals by their starting time before comparing coverage.
Only the last output interval can overlap the next sorted input.
Start a new interval only when start > previous_end; otherwise extend the previous end to the maximum.
approach: Sorting makes starts nondecreasing. Once an interval begins after the end of the current coverage, no later interval can fill that gap, so the current result is complete.

For overlapping or touching intervals, keep the original coverage start and extend only its end. Nested intervals may add no new coverage. Copy endpoints into new rows so extending the result cannot mutate an input row.
complexity: O(n log(n + 1)) time and O(n) extra space including sorted references and output rows.
pitfalls: Assigning an input row directly to the result before modifying it.
Replacing the end with a smaller nested interval endpoint.
transfer: Keep touching intervals separate. Change the comparison and explain how that changes the meaning of coverage groups.

title: Find time for a short appointment
signature: busy: list[list[int]], day_end: int, duration: int
statement: The working day is [0, day_end). Return the earliest integer start where an appointment of duration fits without overlapping any busy interval. Busy intervals are half-open and may overlap, touch or arrive unsorted. Starting when another interval ends is allowed. Return -1 if no slot fits.
constraints: Python 3.11+. Do not mutate any input. All integer inputs exclude bool. Lists and strings have at most 1,000 elements or characters unless stated otherwise.
0 <= day_end <= 1,000,000 and 1 <= duration <= 1,000,000. Every busy row satisfies 0 <= start < end <= day_end.
hints: Track the earliest start not ruled out by the busy intervals already examined.
Sort the intervals; a gap before the next start may fit the appointment.
If candidate + duration <= start, return candidate. Otherwise move candidate to max(candidate, end).
approach: Sorted starts let you inspect free gaps chronologically. Before each busy interval, the candidate is the earliest remaining possible appointment start. If its end is no later than the next busy start, that gap is sufficient.
If the gap is too short, all earlier candidate starts are impossible. Move beyond the busy coverage with max, which also handles nested intervals. After the loop, check the final gap up to day_end.
complexity: O(n log(n + 1)) time and O(n) sorting space for n busy intervals.
pitfalls: Using < instead of <= rejects an appointment that exactly fills a gap.
Moving candidate backward for a nested interval.
transfer: Add a required cleanup gap after each busy interval, clipped at the end of the day.

title: Measure a request burst
statement: Timestamps are sorted integer seconds; duplicates represent separate requests. Return the greatest number of requests that can lie in an interval [s, s + width) for any integer start s. The right boundary is excluded. Return zero for no requests.
constraints: Python 3.11+. Do not mutate any input. All integer inputs exclude bool. Lists and strings have at most 1,000 elements or characters unless stated otherwise.
Timestamps are nondecreasing integers from 0 to 1,000,000. width is from 1 to 1,000,000.
hints: A group fits if its last timestamp minus its first is less than width.
Keep a left endpoint for the oldest request still fitting with the current request.
While timestamps[right] - timestamps[left] >= width, advance left.
approach: For any nonempty set of requests that fits, shifting the interval start to its earliest request still contains that set. It is enough to consider consecutive groups in the sorted list.

When the newest request is width or more seconds after the oldest, those two cannot share a half-open interval. Remove old requests until the group fits, then record its size. Duplicates remain separate positions.
complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Each endpoint advances at most n positions.
pitfalls: Using > instead of >= accidentally includes the excluded right boundary.
Deduplicating timestamps loses distinct requests.
transfer: Return the earliest start of a window achieving the peak as well as its count. Define the empty result.

title: Convert a price into cents
statement: Accept an unsigned decimal price with one to six ASCII digits before the decimal point and, if a point is present, exactly two digits after it. Leading zeros are allowed. No spaces, signs, commas or exponent notation are accepted. Return its integer cents, or None for an invalid string. Examples: "12" gives 1200, "12.05" gives 1205.
constraints: Python 3.11+. Do not mutate any input. All integer inputs exclude bool. Lists and strings have at most 1,000 elements or characters unless stated otherwise.
Input is any ASCII string of at most 100 characters. Invalid strings are part of the task.
hints: Validate the exact grammar before converting any digits.
Split on the decimal point and allow either one or two pieces.
Check lengths and membership in "0123456789", then compute whole * 100 + fraction.
approach: Money enters as text, so preserve its exact decimal meaning. Parsing whole units and cents separately avoids binary floating-point rounding.
Validation must cover every character and the allowed lengths. A missing fractional part means zero cents, while a present but empty or one-digit fractional part is invalid under this grammar.
complexity: O(n) time and O(n) split storage for input length n. Accepted numeric parts have fixed maximum length, so their conversion cost is bounded.
pitfalls: Using float(text) accepts a wider grammar and introduces rounding concerns.
Confusing valid zero cents with the None failure result.
transfer: Allow an optional leading minus for refunds. Specify whether negative zero is preserved or becomes integer zero.

title: Compare numeric release labels
statement: Compare release labels made of dot-separated nonnegative decimal components. Compare components numerically from left to right, treating missing trailing components as zero. Return -1, 0 or 1 when left is smaller, equal or greater. Leading zeros have no special meaning. This is a custom numeric format, not the full Python package-version specification.
constraints: Python 3.11+. Do not mutate any input. All integer inputs exclude bool. Lists and strings have at most 1,000 elements or characters unless stated otherwise.
Each label has 1 to 20 nonempty components. Each component has 1 to 6 ASCII digits. No signs, suffixes or spaces.
hints: String comparison would put 10 before 2.
Convert each component to an integer and compare corresponding positions.
Loop to the longer component count, supplying zero for a missing position.
approach: A release is decided by the first unequal numeric component. Later components matter only if all earlier ones matched, so returning at the first difference implements the ordering directly.
Padding missing trailing positions with zero makes 1 and 1.0 equivalent. Keep this rule separate from real packaging standards, which also define prereleases and other syntax.
complexity: O(c) time and O(c) space for c total input characters, with the stated bounded component size.
pitfalls: Comparing component strings instead of integers.
Assuming more components always means a later release.
transfer: Support a final -preview marker that sorts before its corresponding stable release. Write the comparison rules before implementing it.

title: Plan a small preparation list
statement: Each [task, prerequisite] requires prerequisite to finish before task. Return an order containing every task once. Whenever several tasks are ready, choose the lexicographically smallest name. Repeated requirement rows have no extra effect. Return None if no complete order exists, including a self-dependency. An empty task list has the valid order [].
constraints: Python 3.11+. Do not mutate any input. All integer inputs exclude bool. Lists and strings have at most 1,000 elements or characters unless stated otherwise.
tasks contains at most 100 names, with no duplicates. Each name is a nonempty lowercase ASCII word. Every requirement names two existing tasks. At most 1,000 requirement rows.
hints: A task is ready when every prerequisite already appears in the completed set.
Scan sorted task names for the first unfinished ready task, then repeat.
If no task is ready while unfinished tasks remain, return None.
approach: This small-input solution repeatedly chooses a ready task from sorted names. A set of prerequisites per task removes duplicate requirements without weakening the dependency rule.

Each selected task is safe because all its prerequisites are complete. If none is ready, every unfinished task still depends on unfinished work, so a dependency cycle prevents completion. Rechecking readiness each round also honors the smallest-ready-name rule when new tasks become available.
complexity: With bounded name lengths and expected set operations, O(r + v log(v + 1) + v * (v + e)) worst-case time and O(v + e) extra space for v tasks, r requirement rows and e distinct requirements. Repeated scans favor clarity at v <= 100.
pitfalls: Sorting only the initially ready tasks misses later priority changes.
Returning a partial order without reporting the cycle.
transfer: Replace repeated scans with prerequisite counts and a priority queue of ready tasks. Explain why the output order should remain identical.

title: Process complete stock requests
statement: Each order is [item, quantity]. Process orders in input order using a private working copy of stock. Accept an order only if its entire positive quantity is available, then deduct it. Rejected orders consume nothing. Unknown items have zero stock. Return one boolean per order; leave stock unchanged.
constraints: Python 3.11+. Do not mutate any input. All integer inputs exclude bool. Lists and strings have at most 1,000 elements or characters unless stated otherwise.
ASCII item names. Stock quantities are integers from 0 to 10,000. Order quantities are integers from 1 to 10,000. Each order row has exactly two entries.
hints: You need changing inventory internally without changing the supplied dictionary.
Copy stock once; values are integers, so a shallow copy is sufficient.
Deduct only inside the acceptance branch, then append whether that order succeeded.
approach: Order matters because an accepted request reduces what later requests can use. A private dictionary preserves that state while keeping the function pure from the caller's perspective.

Check the full quantity before deducting anything. Partial fulfillment would change both the returned answer and the inventory available to later requests, so rejection must leave the working quantity unchanged.
complexity: Expected O(s + n + c) time for s stock entries, n orders and c item-name characters examined; O(s) working entries and O(n) output space.
pitfalls: Deducting before checking whether the whole order fits.
Copying the dictionary is essential even though integer values themselves are immutable.
transfer: Allow each order to request several items atomically. Reject the whole order if any item is short.

title: Fit the most optional sessions
statement: Each [start, end] is an optional half-open session. Choose as many sessions as possible without overlaps and return the count. A session may start exactly when the previous one ends. All sessions have equal value; their durations may differ. Identical rows represent competing sessions and cannot both be attended.
constraints: Python 3.11+. Do not mutate any input. All integer inputs exclude bool. Lists and strings have at most 1,000 elements or characters unless stated otherwise.
Each row contains integer times with 0 <= start < end <= 1,000,000. Input may be unsorted.
hints: Choosing the earliest starting session can block many shorter sessions.
Among currently compatible sessions, the one ending earliest leaves the most remaining time.
Sort by end time; accept a session when its start is at least the last accepted end.
approach: Consider the first session of any optimal schedule. Replacing it with the session that ends earliest cannot block a later session, because the replacement finishes no later. This preserves the achievable count.

After accepting that session, the same argument applies to compatible sessions that remain. Sorting by end time lets one forward scan make those choices. This reasoning depends on maximizing count; it does not solve a version with unequal rewards.
complexity: O(n log(n + 1)) time and O(n) sorting space. The selection scan itself uses O(1) auxiliary state.
pitfalls: Choosing shortest duration is not justified by the earliest-finish argument.
Using this greedy rule for unequal session rewards can miss the best total reward.
transfer: Give sessions different integer rewards. Find a counterexample to this greedy rule, then design a method that compares taking and skipping each session.
